Analytic pullback and cotangent directions

Written and self-checked by GPT-6 Astra (OpenAI), Ultra, October 2026. Public domain (CC0).

Composing a distribution with a map requires a condition on directions, not merely on its support. A covector normal to the map can prevent restriction from existing. When those directions are absent, a real analytic map transports every derivative-growth wavefront by its transposed derivative. We prove the estimate for arbitrary maps, obtain equality for changes of coordinates and submersions, and distinguish this sufficient restriction criterion from a necessary condition for every individual example.

We use the Fourier convention , inverse factor , and complex-linear pairings. The supplied Smooth pullback and the Fourier normal condition, Sections 18.1–18.5, contains the existing programme construction, including absolute convergence, Gaussian regularization, cutoff independence, gluing and the smooth wavefront bound. Its source is the AN-03 reading Detecting regularity without choosing coordinates; its complete used sections and prerequisite proofs are available in this reader.

Derivative growth and finite-order localization, Lemma 1 and Theorem 4, gives fixed index shifts and controlled cutoffs. Cones and derivative-growth wavefronts, Theorems 3–7, gives compact conic localization, comparison, singular support and multiplication. Analytic maps and derivative growth, Theorem 3, proves composition for functions. The polydisk Cauchy formula and power-series proof are in Holomorphic boundaries in convex cones, Section 3. Regular level sets and transverse convolution, Lemmas 0.1–0.2 and Theorem 1.1, gives the smooth inverse, coordinate completion and normal Jacobian; Zero hypersurfaces as curvature measures, Lemma 3.0, gives the full measure substitution. These are actual earlier proofs, not external citations in their place.

Analytic coordinates and their inverses

Lemma 3 (analytic local inverse). If a real analytic square map has an invertible derivative at a point, its local inverse is real analytic.

Proof. Translations and an invertible real linear output change reduce the map to , . Extend its convergent series holomorphically to a complex ball. Choose a smaller closed ball on which . For , the map sends that closed ball into its interior and contracts distances by at most . The segment integral proves both estimates in complex coordinates. Starting with , the iterates satisfy , hence converge uniformly in on the smaller ball to a unique fixed point . Completeness and the sum of this geometric series prove convergence directly.

Each iterate is holomorphic in , by the chain rule and the convergent-series definition. On every closed polydisk inside the -ball, the iterates satisfy the polydisk Cauchy formula. Uniform convergence lets the limit pass through its finite contour integrals. Expanding the Cauchy denominators gives a convergent power series for the limit on smaller polydisks, exactly as in the earlier proof. Therefore is holomorphic. For real every iterate is real, so its restriction is real analytic. The fixed-point equation is . Uniqueness implies that maps bijectively onto ; these are open neighborhoods, and the displayed is its inverse. Undo the affine changes.

If a target has dimension zero, its distributions are constants, the pullback is smooth, and all wavefront sets are empty. If the source has dimension zero and the target has positive dimension, condition (11) excludes every nonzero covector at the image point; the singular-support theorem makes locally , so the pullback is its well-defined value. Again there is no nonzero source covector. These conventions also cover the square zero-dimensional identity.

Exercise 4 (advanced: what a failed normal condition does and does not say). For , show why the usual Gaussian pullback of diverges at zero. Contrast this with the ordinary composition of with .

Solution. At zero , so every nonzero target covector is normal. Those are all singular directions of . For a nonnegative compact test near zero, the regularized pairing is

This is the substitution . The integral tends to a finite positive constant by dominated convergence; its tail is bounded by a Gaussian once . The prefactor diverges, so there is no distributional limit along these Gaussian approximations.

In contrast, is analytic. The target has every nonzero wavefront covector at zero: its second distributional derivative is , by two integrations by parts on the half-lines, and the earlier differential inclusion forces both directions into its smooth and every -wavefront. Away from zero it is analytic. The normal condition therefore fails for this target too. Nevertheless its continuous-function composition exists and is analytic. Gaussian convolutions converge uniformly on compact sets to , as follows by splitting the normalized Gaussian integral into a small displacement and a uniformly small first-moment tail; composing with preserves that convergence on compact sets. Thus failure of (11) is not a claim that every particular composition is impossible. It means that this sufficient distributional theorem does not provide it.
